lesson.title: Names that agree
lesson.subtitle: Spaces, capitals, spellings, and one master list

video.title: Names that agree
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Ms Amina Bello — primary teacher, Nigeria (main character)
Mr Joseph — computer studies teacher, Kenya (cameo)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, peer to peer)

scenes.visual: Icon cards: One sheet; Computer: 20; Really: 8. Amina beside it.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Two of us typed the same week's register into one sheet. The computer says my class has twenty pupils. I have eight!

scenes.visual: Paper-grey title card: the Darsi mark, the course name and the lesson title with the Data engineering track chip.
scenes.animation: Mark scales in with a small overshoot; the title slides up.
scenes.narration: Today: making names agree, so that every count comes out right.

scenes.visual: Rows of icon and text: “Amina” ≠ “Aminah”; أ or ا; ة or ه; ى or ي.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: To a computer, two names are the same only if every character matches. So Amina, amina with a space, and Aminah are three different pupils. And in Arabic, one name gets typed with alif or hamza, with ta marbuta or ha.

scenes.visual: Numbered steps: Trim the spaces at the ends; Make the letters the same; Match to the class list.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Clean in order. First, tidy: trim the spaces at the ends, and make the letters the same case. Then match each name to the class list, the one right spelling for every pupil.

scenes.visual: Rows of icon and text: One spelling per pupil; One number per pupil; Everything matches to it.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: That class list is your master list: one agreed spelling and one number for every pupil. Everything else is matched to it, never the other way round.

scenes.visual: Code typed out on a card: names = set() … Caption: A set keeps each name only once
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Python can do the tidying for you. strip removes the spaces at both ends, and lower makes every letter small. Put the clean names in a set, and each name counts only once.

scenes.visual: Rows of icon and text: Name column: a drop-down; No new spellings; Nothing to clean. Mr Joseph beside it.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Prevention beats cleaning. In the sheet, make the name column a drop-down list of the class list. Nobody can type a new spelling, so there's nothing to clean.

scenes.visual: Quiz card: the question with its answer options.
scenes.animation: Answer cards drop in one by one.
scenes.narration: Quick check! A sheet has Musa, musa with a space, and Moussa, all for the same boy. How many pupils does the computer count?

scenes.visual: Icon cards: Three pupils; Tidy fixes one; The list fixes the rest.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.on_screen_text: Every spelling is a new pupil
scenes.narration: Three: every spelling is a different pupil to the computer. Tidying fixes the space and the capital. Only matching to the class list catches Moussa.

scenes.visual: Icon cards joined by arrows: As typed: 20; Tidied: 13; Matched: 8.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: In the app, two teachers typed a week of attendance. Choose how to fix the names: as typed, tidied, or matched to the class list. Watch the names counted fall from twenty to thirteen, then to eight.

scenes.visual: Quiz card: the question with its answer options.
scenes.animation: Answer cards drop in one by one.
scenes.narration: Your turn. Which fix stops new spellings before they even start?

scenes.visual: Summary card: Matched letter by letter; Tidy, then match; One master list; strip() and lower(). Takeaway bar: One spelling per pupil, agreed once.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: A drop-down list: nobody can type a new spelling. Remember: computers match names letter by letter. Tidy, then match to one master list. And in Python, strip and lower do the tidying.

scenes.visual: Rows of icon and text: Ten names, typed many ways; Groups find the same pupil; One spelling, one number. Amina beside it.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Try it in class tomorrow: write ten names on the board as different people typed them. Groups find which ones are the same pupil, and agree one spelling and a number for each. That's your class's master list.

checkpoints.prompt: A sheet has “Musa”, “musa ” and “Moussa”, all for the same boy. How many pupils does the computer count?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — a computer matches letter by letter, so each spelling counts as a different pupil.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — to a computer, any difference, even a space, makes a different name: three pupils.

checkpoints.prompt: Which fix stops new spellings before they start?

options.text: A drop-down list made from the class list
Asking colleagues to type more carefully

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — with a drop-down list, people pick a name instead of typing it, so no new spelling can appear.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — cleaning fixes mistakes after they happen, and care slips. A drop-down list makes them impossible.
